n: When the land is divided, a holy strip is first set apart for the Lord—25,000 by 10,000 units (likely cubits, about 8 by 3 miles). God receives the first portion before the tribes receive theirs.

f.g: An offering or contribution—here a gift of land set apart for God.

n: Within it, the temple occupies a 500-by-500 square with a 50-cubit open buffer around it to protect its holiness.

f.g: Open land or pasture around a site—here a buffer zone.

n: In this holy portion will stand the sanctuary and the most holy place. The temple is literally at the center of Israel’s life.
The priests’ homes are built in this holy area, near the sanctuary they serve.

f.w: the priests the ministers of the sanctuary

n: An equal strip is given to the Levites for their homes and towns. The Greek Old Testament reads “cities to dwell in” instead of “twenty chambers.”

f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; some ancient versions read “towns to live in.”

n: Beside the holy portion lies a strip for the city, belonging to all Israel—not to one tribe. Jerusalem becomes a shared possession.

f.w: it shall be for the whole house of Israel

n: The prince receives land on both sides of the holy area, stretching east and west. His property is defined and limited.

f.w: a portion shall be for the prince

n: Because the prince has his own land, he will no longer seize land from the people. Past kings like Ahab had taken what wasn’t theirs.

f.w: my princes shall no more oppress my people

n: A direct charge to Israel’s rulers: stop violence and robbery, do what is just and right, and end unfair taxation of the people.
Honest weights and measures are required. Cheating with false scales was a common way the powerful exploited the poor.

f.g: A dry measure for grain, about two-thirds of a bushel.
A liquid measure, roughly 6 gallons (22 liters).

n: The ephah (dry) and bath (liquid) are made equal, each one-tenth of a homer—standardizing the system so no one can cheat.

f.g: A large measure, originally a donkey-load—about 6 bushels.

n: Money weights are standardized too: twenty gerahs make a shekel, and sixty shekels make a maneh (mina).

f.g: The smallest unit of weight, about half a gram.

n: The people’s contribution is set: one-sixtieth of their wheat and barley harvest.
Of olive oil, one percent is given—a tenth of a bath from every cor (ten baths).

f.g: A large measure equal to a homer.

n: One lamb from every two hundred is given for offerings that “make reconciliation”—atonement that restores the relationship between God and His people.

f.g: Hebrew kipper—to atone, cover, or reconcile.

n: The whole population brings these gifts to the prince, who will provide the national offerings.
The prince is responsible for providing offerings at all the festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths. Leadership here is service to the community’s worship.

f.g: The first day of each month, marked with offerings.
Wine poured out as an offering.

n: On New Year’s Day, the first day of the first month (spring), a young bull is sacrificed to purify the sanctuary.
The blood is applied to the doorposts of the temple, the altar’s ledge, and the inner gate—like Passover blood on doorposts.

f.w: upon the posts of the house

n: The cleansing is repeated on the seventh day for anyone who sinned by mistake or out of ignorance. God provides for unintentional sins.
Passover is kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, followed by a week of unleavened bread—remembering deliverance from Egypt.
On Passover day the prince provides a sin offering for himself and all the people. Even the ruler needs atonement.
Every day of the feast, seven bulls and seven rams are offered, plus a goat for sin—a lavish, complete offering.

f.g: Seven represents completeness; the amounts differ from Numbers 28:16-25.

n: Grain offerings and oil accompany the animal sacrifices. A hin was about a gallon.

f.g: A liquid measure, roughly a gallon (3.7 liters).

n: The same pattern is followed for the autumn festival on the fifteenth day of the seventh month—the Feast of Tabernacles.

f.w: the feast of the seven days
